title: Data Pipelines and ETL/ELT for Automation
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# Data Pipelines and ETL/ELT for Automation ##### The sync that got slower every week A team synced their CRM into a reporting database nightly. The job truncated the destination table and reloaded everything: 40,000 contacts on day one, taking four minutes. Simple and correct. Eighteen months later it was 900,000 contacts and 70 minutes, and it had started overrunning into business hours. Worse, because it truncated first, any failure left the reporting tables **empty** — analysts arriving at 9 a.m. would occasionally find no data at all. The fix was incremental loading: fetch only records changed since the last successful run, and upsert them. Runtime dropped to eleven seconds, and a failure now left yesterday's data intact rather than nothing. Full reloads are the default because they are easy to reason about. **Incremental loading is what makes a pipeline survive growth**, and getting the mechanics right — watermarks, upserts, deletes, late-arriving data — is the core of this article. ##### ETL versus ELT **ETL** — extract, transform, then load. Transformation happens in your pipeline before data reaches the warehouse. This was necessary when warehouse compute was scarce and expensive. **ELT** — extract, load raw, then transform *inside* the warehouse using SQL. Modern warehouses (BigQuery, Snowflake, and Postgres at moderate scale) have cheap elastic compute, so pushing transformation into them is usually faster and always more flexible. The practical advantage of ELT is **replayability**: because the raw data is preserved, you can fix a transformation bug and rerun it over history without re-extracting from the source. With ETL, a transformation error means the original data is gone and you must re-fetch — assuming the source still has it. The standard modern shape is a three-layer warehouse: ```text raw → exact copy of source data, append-only, never edited staging → cleaned, typed, deduplicated, renamed to canonical fields marts → business-facing models: fact_orders, dim_customers ``` Keep ETL only where you must transform before landing — usually to redact PII or to reduce genuinely enormous volumes. ##### Incremental loads and watermarks A **watermark** records how far you have processed, so the next run resumes rather than restarting. ```sql CREATE TABLE sync_state ( source TEXT PRIMARY KEY, last_watermark TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL, last_run_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), rows_loaded BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 ); ``` ```python OVERLAP = timedelta(minutes=5) # re-read a window to catch late/clock-skewed rows def incremental_sync(source: str, conn) -> int: watermark = conn.fetchval( "SELECT last_watermark FROM sync_state WHERE source = %s", (source,) ) or datetime(1970, 1, 1, tzinfo=UTC) since = watermark - OVERLAP rows, max_seen = [], watermark for page in fetch_pages(source, updated_since=since): for row in page: rows.append(row) max_seen = max(max_seen, row["updated_at"]) if len(rows) >= 1000: upsert(conn, rows); rows.clear() if rows: upsert(conn, rows) # Advance the watermark ONLY after a fully successful load — in the same txn conn.execute( """INSERT INTO sync_state (source, last_watermark, rows_loaded) VALUES (%s, %s, %s) ON CONFLICT (source) DO UPDATE SET last_watermark = EXCLUDED.last_watermark, last_run_at = now(), rows_loaded = EXCLUDED.rows_loaded""", (source, max_seen, len(rows)), ) return len(rows) ``` Three details that matter more than they look. **The overlap window.** Source clocks drift and transactions commit out of order, so a record with `updated_at = 10:00:00` may become visible at 10:00:03 — after a watermark set to 10:00:01. Re-reading a small overlap catches these; the upsert makes the duplicates harmless. **Advance the watermark only on success**, inside the same transaction as the load. Advancing early means a mid-run failure silently skips records forever — the worst kind of data bug, because nothing errors. **Track the maximum `updated_at` actually seen**, not `now()`. Using wall-clock time creates a gap for any record modified during the run. The upsert itself must tolerate re-processing: ```sql INSERT INTO staging.contacts (source_id, email, full_name, source_updated_at, _loaded_at) VALUES %s ON CONFLICT (source_id) DO UPDATE SET email = EXCLUDED.email, full_name = EXCLUDED.full_name, source_updated_at = EXCLUDED.source_updated_at, _loaded_at = now() WHERE staging.contacts.source_updated_at < EXCLUDED.source_updated_at; ``` That `WHERE` guard makes out-of-order arrival safe: an older version of a record cannot overwrite a newer one. ##### Change data capture Watermarks depend on a reliable `updated_at`, and they cannot detect **deletes** — a row removed at the source simply stops appearing, and your copy keeps it forever. **CDC** reads the database's write-ahead log directly, capturing every insert, update and delete as an event. Debezium is the standard implementation; managed options exist in most cloud databases. | | Watermark polling | CDC | |---|---|---| | Detects deletes | No | Yes | | Detects intermediate states | No (only final) | Yes | | Source load | Repeated queries | Minimal (log reader) | | Latency | Poll interval | Near real-time | | Setup complexity | Low | Requires DB access + config | | Works over an API | Yes | Rarely | For SaaS sources you almost always poll, because you have an API rather than database access. For your own databases, CDC is worth the setup when deletes matter or latency requirements are tight. Where you must poll and deletes matter, two workarounds: prefer **soft deletes** at the source (`deleted_at` becomes just another update), or run a periodic **reconciliation** that compares source and destination ID sets and removes orphans. ##### Batch versus streaming **Batch** processes accumulated data on a schedule — simple, cheap, easy to backfill, and correct for anything where minutes or hours of latency are acceptable. Most reporting is batch. **Streaming** processes each event as it arrives — necessary for fraud detection, live dashboards, and anything driving an immediate action. The honest advice: **default to batch**. Streaming multiplies operational complexity — ordering, late data, windowing, state management — and most "real-time" requirements turn out to mean "within fifteen minutes." A **micro-batch** every 5–15 minutes captures most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost. ##### Schema evolution and data quality Sources add fields, rename them, and change types without telling you. Two defences. **Land raw as JSONB.** A new field in the source lands automatically and is available when you decide to use it, rather than breaking the load: ```sql CREATE TABLE raw.contacts ( source_id TEXT NOT NULL, payload JSONB NOT NULL, -- full record, whatever shape _extracted_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (source_id, _extracted_at) ); ``` Staging then projects typed columns out of the JSONB, so a source change breaks a *transformation* you can fix, not an ingestion you cannot. **Validate explicitly** rather than discovering problems in a dashboard. Great Expectations, or dbt tests, or plain SQL assertions: ```yaml # dbt: models/staging/schema.yml models: - name: stg_contacts columns: - name: contact_id tests: [unique, not_null] - name: email tests: - not_null - dbt_utils.expression_is_true: expression: "email LIKE '%@%'" - name: source_updated_at tests: - dbt_utils.expression_is_true: expression: "<= current_timestamp" # no future timestamps tests: - dbt_utils.recency: datepart: hour field: _loaded_at interval: 26 # alert if data is stale ``` That freshness test is the one people omit and most need — it detects a pipeline that stopped running, which no row-level test can. ##### dbt: transformation as engineering **dbt** turns SQL transformations into version-controlled, tested, documented, dependency-aware software. ```sql -- models/marts/fact_orders.sql {{ config(materialized='incremental', unique_key='order_id', on_schema_change='append_new_columns') }} WITH orders AS ( SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_orders') }} {% if is_incremental() %} WHERE _loaded_at > (SELECT COALESCE(MAX(_loaded_at), '1970-01-01') FROM {{ this }}) {% endif %} ), customers AS (SELECT * FROM {{ ref('stg_customers') }}) SELECT o.order_id, o.customer_id, c.email, c.city, o.total_minor / 100.0 AS total_inr, o.placed_at, o._loaded_at FROM orders o LEFT JOIN customers c USING (customer_id) ``` `{{ ref() }}` is what makes this more than a SQL file: dbt builds the dependency graph from those references, so `dbt run` executes models in the correct order and `dbt test` validates the results. Combined with `dbt docs`, you get lineage showing exactly which source feeds which dashboard — the question every data team is asked and few can answer. ##### Connectors: Airbyte and Fivetran **Airbyte** is open-source with 350+ connectors, self-hostable, and free at the extraction layer. **Fivetran** is managed, extremely reliable, and priced per monthly active row — which becomes significant quickly. The economics: building and maintaining a custom connector costs real engineering time, forever. If a connector exists, use it and spend your time on transformation and business logic instead. Write custom extraction only for sources nobody supports. ```mermaid flowchart LR S1[(CRM API)] --> E[Airbyte / n8n
extract] S2[(Postgres)] -->|CDC| E S3[(Files)] --> E E -->|append raw JSONB| R[(raw layer)] R --> D[dbt: staging
clean, type, dedupe] D --> M[dbt: marts
facts + dimensions] D -.tests.-> Q{Quality gate} M -.tests + freshness.-> Q Q -->|fail| A[Alert + halt downstream] Q -->|pass| B[BI dashboards] M --> N[n8n: notify + trigger
business actions] ``` ##### When n8n or Make is enough The genuine decision, and it is not always "use the data stack." **n8n or Make suffices** when volumes are modest (thousands of rows, not millions), the transformation is straightforward field mapping, you need SaaS-to-SaaS movement rather than analytics, business users must maintain it, or the pipeline is inherently event-driven. **Reach for the full stack** when volumes are large, transformations involve multi-table joins and aggregations, you need lineage and documented data quality, analysts want to write SQL against the result, or you must backfill and reprocess history. Hybrid is common and correct: **Airbyte or n8n for extraction, dbt for transformation, and n8n for the business actions the transformed data triggers** — alerts, CRM updates, reports. Use each where it is strongest. ##### Common pitfalls - **Full reloads** that grow linearly and leave tables empty on failure. - **Advancing the watermark before a successful load**, silently skipping records. - **No overlap window**, missing records committed during the previous run. - **Using `now()` as the watermark** instead of the maximum value actually seen. - **Ignoring deletes** in polled syncs, accumulating orphans forever. - **Transforming before landing raw**, making reprocessing impossible. - **No freshness test** — a stopped pipeline looks identical to a quiet source. - **Rigid typed columns at ingestion**, so a new source field breaks the load. - **Streaming by default** where a 15-minute micro-batch would do. - **Custom connectors** for sources Airbyte already supports. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: build an **incremental ELT** — Airbyte or a custom n8n sync into Postgres, then a **dbt transformation**, with a **data-quality check**. Compare the runtime and row count of a full reload against your incremental version on the same source; that difference is the argument for everything in this article. The mini project is that same pipeline with the quality layer taken seriously: not only column tests but a **freshness test** and a row-count anomaly check, wired to an alert. Run it daily and deliberately pause the source for a day to confirm the freshness alert fires. For the assignment, **add CDC-style incremental sync using a watermark so only changed rows load on each run**. Prove it properly: run the sync, note the row count; run it again immediately and confirm zero or near-zero rows load; then modify one source record and confirm exactly one row loads. Also document how you handle deletes, because that is the gap a watermark alone leaves — and being explicit about it is what separates a working pipeline from a correct one. ##### Key takeaways - Prefer ELT with a raw/staging/marts layering — preserving raw data makes transformation bugs fixable by reprocessing rather than re-extracting. - Incremental loading with a watermark is what keeps pipelines fast as data grows; use an overlap window, track the max value seen, and advance only on success. - Watermarks cannot detect deletes — use CDC where you own the database, or soft deletes and periodic reconciliation where you do not. - Land raw as JSONB so schema changes break a transformation you can fix rather than an ingestion you cannot, and test both rows and freshness. - Use existing connectors, transform with dbt for lineage and testing, and keep n8n or Make for modest volumes, event-driven glue and the business actions the data triggers.
